# No-wandering-domain theorem

- [Deutsch](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satz_%C3%BCber_wandernde_Gebiete)
- [Español](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teorema_de_dominio_no_errante)
- [Русский](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%A2%D0%B5%D0%BE%D1%80%D0%B5%D0%BC%D0%B0_%D0%A1%D0%B0%D0%BB%D0%BB%D0%B8%D0%B2%D0%B0%D0%BD%D0%B0_%D0%BE%D0%B1_%D0%BE%D1%82%D1%81%D1%83%D1%82%D1%81%D1%82%D0%B2%D0%B8%D0%B8_%D0%B1%D0%BB%D1%83%D0%B6%D0%B4%D0%B0%D1%8E%D1%89%D0%B8%D1%85_%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%BC%D0%BF%D0%BE%D0%BD%D0%B5%D0%BD%D1%82)
 [Edit links](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Special:EntityPage/Q4455025#sitelinks-wikipedia)                          From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (Redirected from [No wandering domain theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=No_wandering_domain_theorem&redirect=no))  Mathematical theorem

In [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics), the **no-wandering-domain theorem** is a result on [dynamical systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamical_system), proven by [Dennis Sullivan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_Sullivan) in 1985.

The theorem states that a [rational map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_function) *f* : **Ĉ** → **Ĉ** with deg(*f*) ≥ 2 does not have a [wandering domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wandering_set#Wandering_sets_and_dissipative_systems), where **Ĉ** denotes the [Riemann sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_sphere). More precisely, for every [component](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connected_space) *U* in the [Fatou set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatou_set) of *f*, the sequence

     U , f ( U ) , f ( f ( U ) ) , … ,  f  n   ( U ) , …   {\displaystyle U,f(U),f(f(U)),\dots ,f^{n}(U),\dots }

will eventually become periodic. Here, *f* *n* denotes the [*n*-fold iteration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_iteration) of *f*, that is,

      f  n   =     f ∘ f ∘ ⋯ ∘ f  ⏟    n   .   {\displaystyle f^{n}=\underbrace {f\circ f\circ \cdots \circ f} _{n}.}   [![An image of the dynamical plane for f\(z\)=z\+2\\pi\\sin\(z\)\.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/Wandering_domains_for_the_entire_function_f%28z%29%3Dz%2B2%CF%80sin%28z%29.png/250px-Wandering_domains_for_the_entire_function_f%28z%29%3Dz%2B2%CF%80sin%28z%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wandering_domains_for_the_entire_function_f(z)=z+2%CF%80sin(z).png)This image illustrates the dynamics of     f ( z ) = z + 2 π sin ⁡ ( z )   {\displaystyle f(z)=z+2\pi \sin(z)}  ; the Fatou set (consisting entirely of wandering domains) is shown in white, while the Julia set is shown in tones of gray.

The theorem does not hold for arbitrary maps; for example, the [transcendental map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transcendental_function)     f ( z ) = z + 2 π sin ⁡ ( z )   {\displaystyle f(z)=z+2\pi \sin(z)}   has wandering domains. However, the result can be generalized to many situations where the functions naturally belong to a finite-dimensional parameter space, most notably to transcendental entire and meromorphic functions with a finite number of singular values.
